oaf.e: Variant of awf, aufe, probably from Old Norse álfr (“elf”) (whence Norwegian Bokmål alv). Doublet of alf and elf.

s.d: an awkward stupid person
(derogatory) A person, especially a large male, who is clumsy or a simpleton.
x: Ouch! You dropped that box on my feet, you lumbering oaf!

s.d: (dated, derogatory) An ill-mannered person; a boor.
x: I hope you haven't been thinking me an awful oaf for not writing to thank you for so many jolly games after I left Tapsfield?

s.d: (obsolete) An elf's child; a changeling left by fairies or goblins, hence, a deformed or foolish child.

oafish.e:
Etymology tree
English oaf
Proto-Indo-European *-iskos
Proto-Germanic *-iskaz
Proto-West Germanic *-isk
Old English -isċ
Middle English -isch
English -ish
English oafish
From oaf + -ish.

s.d: ill-mannered and coarse and contemptible in behavior or appearance
x: was boorish and insensitive
the loutish manners of a bully

s.d: Characteristic of or resembling an oaf; clumsy, stupid.

oak.e:
Inherited from Middle English ake, hok, oek, ok, oke, from Old English aac, āc, ǣċ, from Proto-West Germanic *aik, from Proto-Germanic *aiks (“oak”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyǵ- (“oak”).
Cognates
From Proto-Germanic: Scots aik, ake, yik (“oak”), North Frisian iake, iik (“oak”), Saterland Frisian Eeke (“oak”), West Frisian iik (“oak”), Cimbrian aicha, oach (“oak”), Dutch eik (“oak”), German Eiche (“oak”), Luxembourgish Eech (“oak”), Vilamovian aach, aeh́, ǡh́ (“oak”), Danish eg (“oak”), Faro

s.d: the hard durable wood of any oak; used especially for furniture and flooring
a deciduous tree of the genus Quercus; has acorns and lobed leaves
x: great oaks grow from little acorns

s.d: A deciduous tree with distinctive deeply lobed leaves, acorns, and notably strong wood, typically of England and northeastern North America, included in genus Quercus.
(uncountable) Any member of species of the genus Quercus, in family Fagaceae.
(uncountable) Any member of other species of trees resembling typical oaks of genus Quercus in some ways.: she-oaks in Allocasuarina and Casuarina, of family Casuarinaceae
(uncountable) The outer (lockable) door of a set of rooms in a college or similar institution. (Often in the phrase sport one's oak.)
x: [E]very set of rooms has two doors, and I soon learned that the outer door, which is thick and solid, is called the oak, and to shut it is termed, to sport.
It was hardly the thing for a master to sport his oak where another member of the staff was concerned.

s.d: To expose to oak in order for the oak to impart its flavors.
Having a rich brown color, like that of oak wood.
Made of oak wood or timber.
x: an oak table, oak beam, etc.

s.d: oak gall caused by larvae of a cynipid wasp
A spherical type of oak gall, produced by an oak gall wasp (tribe Cynipini).
x: [T]he small Apples which I have often observ'd to grow on the leaves of an Oak call'd Oak-apples […] are nothing but the Matrices of an Insect, as I elsewhere show.

s.d: a black plant louse that lives on oaks and dogwoods
a tree of the genus Castanopsis
bright blue-green fern widely distributed especially in damp acid woodlands of temperate Northern Hemisphere
A fern of genus Gymnocarpium (syn. Thelypteris) which grows on trees, especially Gymnocarpium dryopteris.
A bat's wing fern (Histiopteris incisa)
Synonym of common polypody (Polypodium vulgare), a fern formerly thought to have medicinal properties when found growing on an oak.
x: Why say we, that […] to know the vertue of Reubarb, qualitie of Oak ferne, and operation of Polipodie, is only peculiar unto man?

s.d: a deciduous tree of the genus Quercus; has acorns and lobed leaves
x: great oaks grow from little acorns

s.d: annual European plant with spikes of greenish flowers and leaves that are white and hairy on the underside; common as a weed in North America

oaken.e: Inherited from Middle English oken (also eken), from Old English ācen, ǣċen (“of oak”), from Proto-Germanic *aikīnaz, equivalent to oak + -en (adjectival suffix). Cognate with Dutch eiken (“oaken”), German eichen (“oaken”), Icelandic eikinn (“oaken”).

s.d: consisting of or made of wood of the oak tree
x: a solid oak table
the old oaken bucket

s.d: Made from the wood of the oak tree. Also in metaphorical uses, suggesting robustness.
x: Captain Jemmy, taking up three bottles one after another and finding them all empty, ordered up three more, and drew his chair up to the hearth, where he sat kicking the oaken logs viciously with his long legs.
His knuckles are tattooed, his hands the oaken tools of the boxer he still is, now as a coach.

s.d: annual European plant with spikes of greenish flowers and leaves that are white and hairy on the underside; common as a weed in North America

oakum.e: From Late Middle English okom, okome (“oakum”) [and other forms], from Old English ācumba (“oakum”, literally “that which has been combed out, off-combings”) [and other forms], from ācemban (“to comb out”), from Proto-Germanic *uz- (from Proto-Indo-European *ud-s-, *ūd- (“out; up”), or *h₂ew- (“away from, off”)) + *kambijaną (“to comb”) (ultimately from *ǵómbʰos (“row of teeth; tooth; peg”), *ǵembʰ- (“nail; tooth; to gnaw through; to pierce”)). See also out and comb.

s.d: loose hemp or jute fiber obtained by unravelling old ropes; when impregnated with tar it was used to caulk seams and pack joints in wooden ships
(historical, uncountable) Coarse fibres separated by hackling from flax or hemp when preparing the latter for spinning.

(historical, uncountable) Fibres chiefly obtained by untwisting old rope, which are used to caulk or pack gaps between boards of wooden ships and joints in masonry and plumbing, and sometimes for dressing wounds.
x: [N]ow that I think of it, he's always wanting oakum to stuff into the toes of his boots.
Shingle Tiles make a Leak-Proof roof without the use of cements and spun oakums.

oar.e: From Middle English ore (“oar”), from Old English ār, from Proto-West Germanic *airu, from Proto-Germanic *airō (“oar”). Cognate with Old Norse ár.

s.d: an implement used to propel or steer a boat

A type of lever used to propel a boat, having a flat blade at one end and a handle at the other, and pivoted in a rowlock atop the gunwale, whereby a rower seated in the boat and pulling the handle can pass the blade through the water by repeated strokes against the water's resistance, thus moving the boat.
x:
The oar snaps in his hand
Before he reaches dry land
But the sound doesn't deafen his smile
Just pokes at wet sand
With an oar in his hand
Floats off down the river Nile
Floats off down the river Nile...

s.d: An oarsman; a rower.
x: He is a good oar.

s.d: An oar-like swimming organ of various invertebrates.
(literary) To row; to travel with, or as if with, oars.
thin deep-water tropical fish 20 to 30 feet long having a red dorsal fin
A large, greatly elongated, type of fish of the family Regalecidae.
x: For the second time this year an oarfish, a rarely seen deep sea fish that has historically been considered a harbinger of doom, washed up on the California coastline.

s.d: a holder attached to the gunwale of a boat that holds the oar in place and acts as a fulcrum for rowing
A usually U-shaped device attached to the gunwale of a rowboat to hold the oars in place while rowing.
x: But, as luck would have it, scarcely had he started to row his boat again when an oarlock broke, and so it took him the best part of an hour to make the trip.

"No motor," Tranny says. "It snag bad."
 Right. The spiderweb would get wrapped around the propeller. Tranny shows Hiro how to snap zodiac's oars into the oarlocks.

oarsman.e:
Etymology tree
English oar
English -s-
Proto-Indo-European *mon-
Proto-Germanic *mann-
Proto-West Germanic *mann
Old English mann
Middle English man
Middle English -man
English -man
English oarsman
From oar + -s- + -man.

s.d: a male who rows a boat
A person who rows a boat, either alone or with others.
skill as an oarsman
(uncountable) The skill of rowing a boat.

oarswoman.e:
Etymology tree
English oar
English -s-
Proto-Germanic *wībą
Proto-West Germanic *wīb
Old English wīf
Proto-Indo-European *mon-
Proto-Germanic *mann-
Proto-West Germanic *mann
Old English mann
Old English wīfmann
Middle English woman
Middle English -woman
English -woman
English oarswoman
From oar + -s- + -woman.

s.d: a female who rows a boat
A female oarsman.

oasis.e: From Late Latin Oasis, from Ancient Greek Ὄασις (Óasis), from Demotic Egyptian wḥj, from Egyptian wḥꜣt (“oasis, cauldron”), G43-V28-G1-X1:N25 Compare Sahidic Coptic ⲟⲩⲁϩⲉ (ouahe) and Arabic وَاحَة (wāḥa).

s.d: a fertile tract in a desert (where the water table approaches the surface)
a shelter serving as a place of safety or sanctuary
A spring of fresh water, surrounded by a fertile region of vegetation, in a desert.
x: It was now a beautiful, moonlit night. The air was crisp and invigorating. Behind them lay the interminable vista of the desert, dotted here and there with an occasional oasis.
On the edge of the dunes lies the oasis town of Dunhuang, a key strategic crossroads on the Silk Road as the routes divided to the west to skirt the Taklamakan to the north and south.

s.d: (figuratively) A quiet, peaceful place or situation separated from surrounding noise or bustle.
x: The park was an oasis in the middle of the busy city.

s.d: (figuratively) A place or situation of fruitfulness or abundance separated from surrounding barrenness or scarcity.

oast.e: From Middle English ost, from Old English āst (“a kiln”), from Proto-Germanic *aistaz (“kiln”), from *aisǭ (“fire”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eydʰ- (“to burn; fire”). Cognate with Dutch eest (“kiln”), Middle Low German eiste (“kiln”), Latin aedes (“house; hearth”), Old English ād (“fire; funeral pyre”).

s.d: a kiln for drying hops
a building containing an oast (a kiln for drying hops); usually has a conical or pyramidal roof
(UK) A building containing oasts, used in conjunction with hop harvesting.

oat.e:
Inherited from Middle English ote, from Old English āte, from Proto-West Germanic *aitā, from Proto-Germanic *aitǭ (“swelling; gland; nodule”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyd- (“to swell”). See English atter (“poison”).
Cognates
* Germanic: cognate with Scots ait (“oat”), West Frisian oat (“wild oat”), Dutch oot, aat (“wild oat”), Saterland Frisian Aate (“pea”), German Low German Aat (“oat”), obsolete Luxembourgish Otz (“oat”). Further related to Icelandic eitill (“nodule”), Norwegian Bokmål ei

s.d: annual grass of Europe and North Africa; grains used as food and fodder (referred to primarily in the plural: ‘oats’)
seed of the annual grass Avena sativa (spoken of primarily in the plural as ‘oats’)
(uncountable) Widely cultivated cereal grass, typically Avena sativa.
x: The oat stalks made good straw.
The main forms of oat are meal and bran.

s.d: Any of the numerous species, varieties, or cultivars of any of several similar grain plants in genus Avena.
x: The wild red oat is thought to be the ancestor of modern food oats.

s.d: (uncountable) The seeds of the oat, a grain, harvested as a food crop and for animal feed.
x: […]I could munch your good dry Oates. Me-thinkes I haue a great deſire to a bottle of hay: good hay, ſweete hay hath no fellow.

s.d: (uncountable) A simple musical pipe made of oat-straw.
(uncountable) The tiniest amount; a whit or jot.
x: Few of them care an oat for the niceties of the arrow sport, but for the young lords that may be on a hunt!

s.d: highly malignant carcinoma composed of small round or egg-shaped cells with little cytoplasm; lung cancers are frequently oat cell carcinomas
thin flat unleavened cake of baked oatmeal
Any of many flat biscuits, or cakes, made from oatmeal.

oaten.e: Inherited from Middle English oten, *aten (“oaten”); equivalent to oat + -en. Cognate with Scots aiten (“oaten”).

s.d: of or related to or derived from oats
x: oaten bread

s.d: Of, pertaining to, or made of oats.
x: an oaten cake

oath.e:
From Middle English ooth, oth, ath, from Old English āþ (“oath”), from Proto-West Germanic *aiþ (“oath”), from Proto-Germanic *aiþaz (“oath”).
Cognate with Scots aith, athe (“oath”), North Frisian ith, iss (“oath”), Saterland Frisian Eed (“oath”), West Frisian eed (“oath”), Dutch eed (“oath”), German Eid (“oath”), Swedish ed (“oath”), Icelandic eið (“oath”), Latin ūtor (“make use of, employ, avail”, verb), Old Irish óeth (“oath”).

s.d: profane or obscene expression usually of surprise or anger
x: expletives were deleted

s.d: a commitment to tell the truth (especially in a court of law); to lie under oath is to become subject to prosecution for perjury
a solemn promise, usually invoking a divine witness, regarding your future acts or behavior
x: they took an oath of allegiance

s.d: A solemn pledge or promise that invokes a deity, a ruler, or another entity (not necessarily present) to attest the truth of a statement or sincerity of one's desire to fulfill a contract or promise.
x: take an oath
swear an oath

s.d: A statement or promise which is strengthened (affirmed) by such a pledge.
x: After taking the oath of office, she became the country's forty-third premier.
The generals swore an oath of loyalty to the country.

s.d: A light, irreverent or insulting appeal to a deity or other entity.
A curse, a curse word.
x: The farther from the Senator's office, the darker and older the furniture, the freer fly four-letter oaths, the higher the heaps of unfiled and unattended papers culminating in a frenzy of pulp in the press section[…]

s.d: (archaic) To pledge.

oatmeal.e: From Middle English otemele, from ote (“oat”) + mele (“meal, coarse-ground grains”). Equivalent to oat + meal.

s.d: porridge made of rolled oats
meal made from rolled or ground oats
(uncountable) A breakfast cereal made from rolled oats, cooked in milk or water.
(uncountable) A light greyish brown colour, like that of oatmeal.
Of a light greyish brown colour, like that of oatmeal.
x: Boldly patterned textiles in oatmeal tones with a woven design in a strongly contrasting colour can be used alike for upholstery and as a wall hanging […]

s.d: cookies containing rolled oats
A cocktail consisting of Irish cream, Goldschläger, and butterscotch schnapps.
